title: Fault-tolerant quantum interconnects that let processors scale by adding modules

concept.text: The innovation would let separate quantum processor modules operate together as one larger, error-corrected quantum computer. Each module would hold logical qubits—quantum information protected by error correction—and the interconnect would support reliable operations between logical qubits in different modules. The target is sustained computation across processor boundaries, with errors suppressed by the combined local and intermodule error-correction system.

In architectures that use shared entanglement, the link must continually supply usable Bell pairs: pairs of qubits whose joint quantum state provides a resource for operations between modules. Their delivery rate must keep pace with the chosen circuit’s consumption after losses and protocol overheads, while their errors remain manageable by the chosen code. Physical state transfer, a remote physical gate or an entangled pair is an enabling step; the proposed innovation integrates those capabilities into protected logical computation.

significance.text: A working modular interconnect would offer a route beyond the capacity of a single chip, crystal or vacuum chamber. Individual modules face fabrication, packaging, control and environmental constraints. Reliable logical connections could allow a computation to use the combined capacity of several modules, making it possible to execute circuits whose required logical resources exceed those available in any one module.

The analogy with expanding a classical data center by adding machines captures the intended architectural change, but it has limits. A successful two-module logical link would not establish unrestricted scaling. More modules would also require suitable network topology, adequate aggregate bandwidth, coordinated control and reliable local logical operations. The connection must remain useful as communication demand grows, rather than merely work for an isolated remote operation.

Intermodule operations could also support nonlocal error-correction checks for codes whose connectivity requirements are difficult to accommodate inside one module. The superconducting-interconnect paper connects distributed entangling operations with prospective large-scale quantum low-density parity-check code implementations. This benefit depends on the code and network design; a link alone does not establish a practical error-correction advantage.

Scope synthesis: a city-scale or continental quantum internet would be a further communications achievement, requiring capabilities beyond a computing interconnect between nearby modules. Quantum repeaters, secure key distribution and distributed sensor networks have related communication needs, but success at modular logical computation would not by itself establish those applications or their practical performance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the supplied demonstrations is sustained, error-suppressed logical operation across modules. Rate and fidelity are separate constraints, rather than a universally meaningful product of rate times fidelity. A fast link can deliver too many errors, while a high-fidelity link can leave the computation waiting. Required Bell-pair consumption depends on the algorithm, error-correcting code, logical clock and intermodule protocol; there is no universal number of pairs required per logical cycle.

Concrete interface barriers include qubit coherence during transfer, qubit-to-cable coupling and cable loss for superconducting microwave links, and conversion losses and probabilistic entanglement generation for the demonstrated photonic interface. Their combined effect must be evaluated at the point where entanglement becomes usable by the computation. Timing conventions matter: a generation rate that excludes characterization readout does not describe the same experimental cycle as a rate that includes generation and measurement.

The engineering challenge extends from the physical link to its encoded interface. Increasing the relevant error-correction resources must reduce end-to-end logical error despite interface faults and communication delays, while leaving enough usable throughput for sustained computation. An architecture need not assign a literal code distance to the transmission medium: protection may instead be implemented through encoded endpoints and intermodule protocols. The decisive issue is whether the complete operation becomes more reliable as its protection increases.

current_state.text: The supplied research dates Neereja M. Sundaresan and collaborators’ preprint, “Meter-scale quantum interconnects between large quantum processors,” to 21 October 2026. It reports four L-couplers, each using 80 cm of coaxial cable, between two 120-qubit IBM processors. Across the four couplers, the reported mean network-benchmarked state-transfer fidelity is 99.00%, and the mean distant controlled-Z gate fidelity is 94.75%. Only a subset of the processors’ qubits was wired and measured, so the nominal processor sizes do not mean that all 240 qubits participated in the interconnect experiment.

These superconducting results demonstrate physical transfer and distant physical gates. The transfer benchmark incorporates qubit coherence, qubit-cable coupling and cable loss into its reported performance. The experiment does not report an encoded logical interconnect or decreasing intermodule logical error with increasing error-correction resources. Its meter-scale framing reflects module cryogenic environments and classical signal delivery; the reported coaxial length is 80 cm per coupler.

The supplied research dates Lukas Hartung, Pierre Barral, Matteo Pompili and collaborators’ preprint, “Quantum Networking at the Speed of Quantum Computation,” to 9 October 2026 and supplies its version-2 HTML text. It reports Bell pairs between an ion and a silicon-vacancy center at an average generation rate of 1.03(1) kHz and fidelity of 87.9(7)%, including conversion losses. The demonstration entangles individual physical matter qubits; it does not demonstrate two error-corrected computational modules. The reviewed supplement also states that no quantum information is stored on the nuclear spin in this demonstration.

The 1.03(1) kHz rate excludes a 664-microsecond characterization-readout step. Including that step gives a wall-clock rate of 612(4) Hz for generated and measured pairs. The higher figure therefore describes generation under a particular timing convention, while the lower figure describes the measured experimental sequence. Neither figure alone establishes the throughput of a future encoded computational protocol.

The photonic paper cites estimates of 10–100 kHz for continuous logical operations between modules under assumptions about known algorithms, plausible near-term qubit fidelities and error-correction schemes. Its reported 1.03 kHz generation rate is approximately 9.7–97 times below that range, reasonably rounded to about 10–100 times. This comparison identifies a throughput gap under those assumptions; it is not a universal threshold, and closing it would still leave the task of achieving suitable error rates and demonstrating logical operation.

Both supplied experimental reports are preprints, and neither demonstrates the proposed fault-tolerant logical interconnect. The supplied review had a complete 11-page extraction for the superconducting paper. For the photonic paper, the retained HTML extraction was truncated at the trailing footer, while the relevant main text and supplementary passages were available. An optional PDF retained under that source was actually a fiber datasheet and provides no evidence for the Bell-pair results; that mismatch does not invalidate the separately reviewed HTML evidence.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material contains no comprehensive freshness search establishing the worldwide state as of 1 November 2026. These dated experiments establish the scope of their reported achievements, not that every other effort remains below the proposed target. No continental-repeater result is supplied for assessment, so no conclusion about such a result’s existence or performance follows from this record.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: entangle logical qubits held in two separate processor modules through a link of at least meter scale, and show decreasing end-to-end logical error as the relevant module and intermodule error-correction resources increase. The distance is a proposed engineering benchmark, motivated by module-scale interconnection, rather than an established requirement. The protection test should describe the actual encoded interface instead of requiring an undefined code distance on the transmission medium.
completion_criteria.label: Meter-scale two-module logical entanglement whose end-to-end error falls as resources increase

completion_criteria.text: Proposed operational test: sustain logical two-qubit gates across the modules throughout a circuit whose required logical capacity exceeds either module alone. Measure usable entanglement delivery and consumption after the overheads of the implemented protocol, and demonstrate that delivery keeps pace. Report both logical reliability and elapsed execution time, so a brief burst of successful operations cannot substitute for sustained integration. A mean physical controlled-Z fidelity in the mid-90% range, without logical encoding, would not meet this proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Delivery keeps pace for logical two-qubit circuits exceeding either module

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scaling evidence: publish enough detail about the encoding, interface, timing, losses, error estimation and workload to permit replication, and reproduce the logical-error trend across repeated runs. Extending the demonstration to additional modules or network arrangements would test whether aggregate throughput and control remain adequate as the system grows. Report the distances, module counts, protection levels and workload classes actually tested. Finite experiments establish demonstrated breadth and practical boundaries; they cannot establish literal universality or unlimited scaling.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduced logical-error trend with replication detail and stated practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis—QUA-01, “Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation,” concerns the broader ability to suppress errors while performing universal logical computation. QUA-06 addresses the intermodule connection needed for a modular implementation of that goal. QUA-08, “Local, universal fault tolerance whose overhead stays bounded as the error falls,” adds a distinct locality and overhead target. A successful QUA-06 interconnect would not by itself establish either universal logical computation or bounded overhead.

Roster synthesis—QUA-02, “Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm,” QUA-03, “Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter,” and QUA-09, “An end-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on large classical data,” are computational outcome targets that might benefit from greater modular capacity. An interconnect demonstration would not establish cryptographic scale, experimentally verified material predictions or an end-to-end speedup. Those entries retain their own algorithm, validation and resource requirements.

Roster synthesis—QUA-04, “A laboratory material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature,” and QUA-05, “Universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons,” concern distinct approaches to storage and computation. They could overlap with future modular architectures if suitable interfaces were developed, but passive memory protection or braiding-based computation does not itself demonstrate a fault-tolerant intermodule link. Conversely, QUA-06 does not require either mechanism.

Roster synthesis—QUA-07, “A proof that quantum polynomial time exceeds classical polynomial time on decision problems,” is a mathematical complexity separation. Successful modular hardware would not supply that proof. QUA-10, “Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator,” concerns fabrication and operating conditions. QUA-06 can be pursued with cryogenic processors, as in the supplied superconducting experiment, and does not establish the manufacturing or temperature requirements of QUA-10.

change_log.change: Replaced the rate-times-fidelity formulation with separate throughput and error constraints, and made Bell-pair demand architecture dependent.
change_log.reason: The review supports joint rate and fidelity requirements but no universal product metric or fixed pair consumption per logical cycle.

change_log.change: Integrated the modular-scaling motivation with explicit connectivity, bandwidth, control and error-correction conditions.
change_log.reason: The data-center analogy explains the potential impact but cannot establish effortless or unlimited scaling.

change_log.change: Preserved all principal superconducting performance numbers while specifying four L-couplers, 80 cm of coax per coupler and partial processor wiring.
change_log.reason: Two nominally 120-qubit processors do not imply that all their qubits participated in the measured interconnect.

change_log.change: Clarified that the ion–silicon-vacancy experiment connects physical matter qubits, and added the readout-inclusive 612(4) Hz rate and 664-microsecond readout duration.
change_log.reason: The original account obscured experimental scope and the timing convention behind the 1.03(1) kHz generation rate.

change_log.change: Retained the approximately 10–100-fold rate comparison while explaining its assumptions and its separation from fidelity and logical operation.
change_log.reason: The numerical comparison is supported, but the cited 10–100 kHz range is not a universal completion threshold.

change_log.change: Recast completion around end-to-end logical error suppression, sustained workload execution and reproducibility, with meter-scale distance explicitly proposed.
change_log.reason: An architecture-neutral encoded-interface test avoids an undefined requirement for code distance on the link.

change_log.change: Replaced the unsupported research-pass search-history assertion with a bounded statement about the supplied evidence.
change_log.reason: The empty freshness record establishes neither a comprehensive November 2026 status nor what continental-repeater sources were searched or opened.

change_log.change: Preserved extraction limitations and excluded the misidentified fiber-datasheet PDF from experimental support.
change_log.reason: The valid photonic HTML evidence remains usable, while the unrelated PDF cannot corroborate it.

change_log.change: Added explicit distinctions for every other supplied roster entry and separated local computing interconnects from long-distance communications.
change_log.reason: Related hardware, application and mathematical goals overlap with modular computing without being equivalent to it.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the comprehensive worldwide state as of 1 November 2026 or assess any continental-repeater result.

The practical entanglement rate and tolerated errors remain dependent on the selected code, workload, logical clock and intermodule protocol; the cited 10–100 kHz estimate does not resolve those choices.

The proposed meter-scale distance, workload and resource-scaling tests are not established standards. Architecture-specific implementation details and convincing quantitative acceptance thresholds remain to be defined.
Scaling beyond two modules remains an open demonstration requirement, including aggregate bandwidth, topology, coordinated control and end-to-end logical reliability.
The photonic evidence relies on the reviewed HTML extraction, whose footer was truncated. Its retained optional PDF is unrelated, so it supplies no independent paper-PDF corroboration.

brief.title: Quantum computers that grow by adding modules
possible: Researchers could run a quantum calculation too large for any single processor by connecting smaller modules. Each would hold logical qubits, units of quantum information protected by error correction. Reliable connections would let them compute together as a larger machine.
why: Quantum computers face limits on how much hardware can fit and work inside a chip or chamber. Connecting modules would give researchers a route beyond those limits, using their combined capacity for larger calculations.

sources.who: Neereja M. Sundaresan and collaborators at IBM Research
sources.showed: The team transferred quantum information between processors and built controlled-Z (CZ) gates, operations linking qubits arranged on separate chips. Fidelity measures how accurately an operation works.
sources.quote:
we construct distant CZ gates between lattice qubits
on separate processors at a mean fidelity of 94.75%
sources.cited_for: Superconducting cables can carry quantum information and support operations between processor modules.
sources.not_established: The experiment did not connect protected logical qubits or show errors falling as protection increased.

sources.who: Lukas Hartung, Pierre Barral and collaborators at IonQ and Duke University
sources.showed: The team linked an ion, a charged atom, with a silicon-vacancy (SiV) defect in diamond. They created Bell pairs, qubits sharing a joint quantum state; kHz means thousands of pairs per second.
sources.quote:
Including all conversion losses, we generate ion–SiV
-
Bell pairs at an average rate of 1.03(1) kHz
sources.cited_for: Light can connect different kinds of physical qubits while accounting for losses in converting the light.
sources.not_established: The experiment did not connect error-corrected processors, and its generation rate excluded measurement time.

shown: IBM Research and the IonQ-led team have demonstrated physical building blocks for connected quantum processors. Both reports are preprints. Neither demonstrates sustained computation protected against errors across processor boundaries.
missing: A complete connection must become more reliable as error-correction resources increase, despite faults and delays along the link.
Usable shared quantum states must arrive fast enough to sustain a calculation after losses and protocol overheads.
Larger networks must maintain enough communication capacity and coordinated control as more modules join.

milestones.label: Protected quantum links with errors that fall
milestones.explanation: Logical qubits at least a meter apart would have to share a joint quantum state, with errors falling as protection increases. This would establish that error correction works across the complete connection.

milestones.label: Sustained calculations larger than a module
milestones.explanation: A calculation exceeding either module’s capacity would have to sustain operations linking logical qubits across modules, with delivery keeping pace and reliability and elapsed time measured. This would establish useful combined computation.

milestones.label: Repeatable error reduction with clear practical boundaries
milestones.explanation: Repeated runs would have to reproduce falling logical errors, with enough detail for replication and clear limits on tested systems and workloads. Testing added modules or network layouts would probe how far the result extends.

uncertain: The required delivery rate and tolerated errors depend on the calculation, error-correction scheme and communication protocol.
The proposed distance and workload tests are not established standards; convincing acceptance thresholds remain to be defined.
